title: 1945 decision whether to re-authorize or pause a second atomic city attack after Hiroshima and Soviet entry

decision_cutoff.date_or_period: Before 03:47 Tinian time on 9 August 1945 (17:47 UTC / 13:47 Washington Eastern War Time on 8 August); precise actionable instant unresolved
decision_cutoff.definition: Senior U.S. civilian/military authority considering whether to allow the standing repeated-use directive to proceed before the second mission departs. Stimson supplied Hiroshima damage reports to Truman during a meeting whose body places it about11:15-noon Washington time on8August. The inspected Soviet-entry records do not establish responsible-authority receipt before the departure bound, nor a usable command-and-communications stop window. This case is not admitted as a verified combined-shock historical replay.

packets.masking_note: Audit packet naming Hiroshima, Japan, Soviet entry and the standing U.S. atomic-use directive.

Countries, cities, weapon name and dates removed; the structure of a prior standing authorisation, first catastrophic use, new allied belligerent entry, continuing non-surrender and imminent second irreversible attack is retained.

expected_constitutional_constraints: A standing authorisation for repeated irreversible force must not become morally self-renewing when material facts change.
The decision must distinguish absence of surrender from evidence that immediate second city use is necessary before newly changed conditions can have effect.
Foreseeable civilian mass harm requires a high burden of necessity, proportionality and alternative assessment.
Senior authorities remain accountable for delegated operational action and should not evade reassessment merely because an earlier order technically permits continuation.
Delay itself has costs in an ongoing war; reassessment cannot assume waiting is harmless or that surrender is imminent without evidence.
Hiroshima and the second-use decision are separate cases because the evidence state has materially changed.

sources.citation: National Security Archive, July 1945 atomic-use directive and related messages
sources.use_note: Documents that the July directive authorized the first attack and stated additional bombs would be delivered on listed targets as soon as made ready.

sources.citation: Groves, Plan of Operations – Atomic Fission Bomb, 24 July 1945
sources.use_note: Shows repeated-bomb planning, target structure and anticipated follow-on deliveries.

sources.citation: Memorandum of Conference with the President, 8 August 1945
sources.use_note: Primary scanp1: title10:45AM; body says arrival about11:15 and exit aboutnoon. Damage reports and photographs were shown to Truman. No inference of Soviet-entry receipt follows from this meeting.

sources.citation: National Security Archive, Far Eastern War and General Situation, 8 August 1945
sources.use_note: Primary scanp1 records Harriman, Kennan, Stalin and Molotov in Moscow and Soviet military reports; it does not record a Washington receipt time. Kept for research, not proof of predeparture U.S. senior-authority knowledge.

sources.citation: National Museum of the United States Air Force, The Mission
sources.use_note: Confirms the second mission departed before dawn 9 August, primary target Kokura and secondary Nagasaki. Outcome details are reserved for reveal.

sources.citation: National Security Archive, Admiral Takagi diary and August 8-9 Japanese decision records
sources.use_note: Shows that Japan had not surrendered after Hiroshima and that hard-line resistance remained significant. Internal Japanese information not demonstrably available to U.S. decision-makers is not used as pre-decision U.S. evidence.

sources.citation: Handy to Spaatz, atomic-use directive, primary scan
sources.use_note: Scan dated25July; catalogue says26July. Paragraph2 authorises follow-on bombs; paragraph4 names Secretary of War and Chief of Staff approval.

sources.citation: Grew memorandum of conversation, FRUS1945volVI doc402
sources.use_note: Informal notice at14:50Washington; later than reconstructed13:47departure bound. Does not prove no earlier channel.

sources.citation: Truman news conference, Official Reporter note
sources.use_note: 15:00Washington announcement proves knowledge by then, not earlier receipt before departure.

sources.citation: National Park Service, atomic bombing timeline
sources.use_note: Departure entry0347Tinian, one hour ahead of Japan. Converted toUTC17:47 andWashington13:47,8August. Primary mission log and effective stop-order deadline unverified; later attack outcomes excluded.
